clips.title: Section 1: Registering a child for summer camp

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: Good morning, Greenfield Summer Camp. How can I help you?

lines.speaker: Mrs Doyle
lines.text: Hello, I would like to register my daughter for the summer camp, please.

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: Of course. Could I take your surname first?

lines.speaker: Mrs Doyle
lines.text: It is Doyle, D-O-Y-L-E.

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: Thank you, Mrs Doyle. And how old is your daughter?

lines.speaker: Mrs Doyle
lines.text: Her name is Sophie, and she has just turned nine.

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: The camp runs two sessions each day: a morning session and an afternoon session.

lines.speaker: Mrs Doyle
lines.text: We first thought about the morning session, but the afternoon session is better, because she has piano lessons at ten o'clock.

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: Children also choose one main activity for the whole week: swimming, art classes or outdoor games.

lines.speaker: Mrs Doyle
lines.text: Sophie said art classes at first, but she changed her mind this morning. She wants the outdoor games now.

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: The fee is 120 pounds for each week, and there is a discount of ten per cent on the second week.

lines.speaker: Mrs Doyle
lines.text: She will come for two weeks, starting on Monday the seventh of July.

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: For lunch, children can bring a packed lunch, or buy a hot lunch at the camp kitchen for four pounds a day.

lines.speaker: Mrs Doyle
lines.text: She will bring a packed lunch, except on Fridays, when she can have the hot lunch as a treat.

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: Finally, could I have an emergency contact number?

lines.speaker: Officer
lines.text: Thank you. We will send the confirmation letter by email this week.

clips.title: Section 2: An introduction to Highmoor National Park

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: Welcome to this short guide to Highmoor National Park, one of the largest protected areas in the north of the country.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: The park covers 850 square kilometres, and it welcomes around two million visitors every year.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: Most visitors start at the main visitor centre in the village of Kirkby, where parking costs five pounds per day.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: From the centre, a shuttle bus takes visitors to the famous waterfall every hour, and the journey takes twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: The highest point in the park is Highmoor Peak, which rises to 724 metres above sea level.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: Guided walks used to leave the centre at ten o'clock, but from this month they leave at nine thirty, so that walkers avoid the midday heat.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: Dogs are welcome in most areas, but near the lake, where rare birds are nesting, they must be kept on a lead.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: The park is well known for its red deer, and the best place to see them is the valley below the old stone bridge.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: If you stay overnight, the campsite near the forest has space for sixty tents, and booking is essential in August.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: Inside the visitor centre, a new exhibition about the park's wildlife has just opened, and entry is free for members.

lines.speaker: Presenter
lines.text: Finally, always check the weather forecast before you set off, because conditions on the hills can change very quickly.

clips.title: Section 3: Planning a group assignment on local transport

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: Thanks for coming, both of you. Let us look at the plan for your group assignment on local transport.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: We have decided to compare bus services in two towns, Marlow and Henby.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: I will collect data on passenger numbers at the main stops.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: And I will interview some of the bus drivers about their routes.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: Good. Remember that the assignment must be no longer than four thousand words.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: At first we hoped to interview ten drivers, but only six agreed to take part.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: We also planned five sections, but we have cut it down to four, to keep within the word limit.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: That sounds sensible. When will the first draft be ready?

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: We aimed for the fifteenth of May, but the library data arrives late, so the draft will be ready on the twenty-second of May.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: I am a bit worried about the statistics section, because the software is new to me.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: The university runs a free workshop on that software every Wednesday afternoon in the computer lab.

lines.speaker: Jake
lines.text: We would also like to include photographs of the bus stations in the report.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: That is fine, but you must ask the transport company for permission before you use any photographs.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: We will meet again next Tuesday, and we will send you the outline by Friday.

clips.title: Section 4: A lecture on the history of writing

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: In this lecture, I will follow the development of writing, from the first marks pressed into clay to the printed book.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: The earliest known system of writing is cuneiform, which appeared in Mesopotamia around 3400 BC.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Cuneiform was used mainly by officials to keep records of goods, such as grain and animals.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: The signs were pressed into wet clay tablets using a reed, and the tablets were then dried in the sun.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: At about the same time, the Egyptians developed hieroglyphs, which they carved into stone and painted on tomb walls.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Unlike cuneiform, hieroglyphs were also used for religious purposes in temples.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Many centuries later, the Phoenicians created an alphabet with only twenty-two signs.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Because the system was so small, ordinary traders could learn it, not just trained scribes.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: The Greeks took this alphabet and added separate signs for vowel sounds, which made texts easier to read aloud.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Paper reached Europe from China, where it had been invented many centuries before.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Before paper arrived, Europeans wrote on parchment, a material made from animal skin.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Making just one book took the skins of about fifty sheep, so books stayed rare and expensive for centuries.
